summary: Provides a list of terms used in the IETF when discussing internationalization, to help frame discussions and introduce key concepts to participants. It is a best current practice.

eli5.summary: Writing words from many languages on computers brings in many special terms. This is a glossary so everyone at the table uses the same words.

questions: what is internationalization in the ietf
what is the difference between a charset and a script
what is an ace in idna
subtitle: A shared glossary so IETF working groups mean the same thing when they talk about languages, scripts, characters and encodings.

tldr.problem: Internationalization is discussed in many IETF working groups, few of which have experts, and terms like character, charset and variant get used loosely.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is a glossary. It defines terms such as script, coded character set, charset, normalization, collation and bidirectional display, notes where common usage is confusing, and gives the source of each definition.
tldr.outcome: IETF standards SHOULD use these definitions unless they explicitly provide others. This RFC obsoletes RFC 3536.

facts.label: UTF-8 length
facts.value: 1 to 3 octets in the BMP, 4 outside

today: RFC 6365 is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 3536. The unit metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Format of the Glossary
sections.content:
The RFC starts from a line in the IETF character set policy (RFC 2277): "Internationalization is for humans." Protocols are not internationalized; the text strings in them are. Anyone should be able to enter and read those strings, in any human language.

The glossary exists to help frame discussions and introduce key concepts to IETF participants. Working groups often ask "Should we internationalize this?" without an expert in the room. The definitions SHOULD be used by IETF standards. A standard that wants different definitions can supply them, but is encouraged to choose different terms for clarity.

Each definition shows its source in angle brackets, such as <UNICODE>, and <RFC6365> means the definition was written for this document. Examples use Unicode notation such as U+0061 for the letter "a".
sections.eli5: It is a dictionary for people who design internet rules, so they all use the same words for the same ideas.

sections.title: Fundamental Terms
sections.content:
A script is a set of graphic characters used to write one or more languages, such as Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic and Han. A language is a way humans communicate. Novices mix them up: Russian and Bulgarian are both written in Cyrillic, Mongolian can use either the Mongolian or Cyrillic script, and Japanese normally mixes Kanji, Katakana and Hiragana in one string. Most protocols that handle non-ASCII text deal with scripts or characters rather than languages.

A coded character set (CCS) is a set of rules that establishes a character set and how its characters map to coded representations. A character encoding scheme (CES) is an encoding form plus byte serialization, such as UTF-8 and UTF-16BE. A charset maps a sequence of octets to a sequence of abstract characters, in effect one or more CCSs combined with a CES. The RFC prefers "charset" over "character set", which has other meanings outside the IETF.

In the IETF, internationalization (abbreviated i18n) means adding or improving the handling of non-ASCII text in a protocol. Localization (l10n) is adapting an application to a specific cultural environment, and is rarely an IETF matter. If multiple charsets are allowed they must be identified, and the RFC says the best way today is usually to allow only Unicode encoded in UTF-8.
sections.eli5: A script is a set of letters, like the alphabet you use, and a language is what you say with them. Many languages can share one alphabet, and one language can use several.

sections.title: Standards Bodies, Encodings and Charsets
sections.content:
Two groups define the characters. ISO/IEC 10646 is the ISO/IEC standard whose CCS covers almost all known written characters in use. The Unicode Consortium publishes the Unicode Standard, a CCS whose repertoire and code points are identical to ISO/IEC 10646 and which adds character properties such as case conversion. The two track each other for assignments. The IETF used to prefer citing ISO/IEC 10646, but now prefers the Unicode Standard because IETF specifications depend on its property definitions.

The Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) is the first 2^16 code points. UCS-2 addresses only the BMP and is considered obsolete by many. UTF-8 (RFC 3629) is the preferred encoding for IETF protocols: BMP characters take one, two or three octets, characters outside the BMP take four, and US-ASCII characters keep their ASCII representation. UTF-16 and UTF-32 are not required by any IETF standard.

Before ISO/IEC 10646 many countries built their own CCSs and charsets, for example ISO 8859-5 for Cyrillic and Shift-JIS for Japanese. IANA keeps the registry of charset names. ASCII is strictly a CCS and repertoire, not an encoding; the IETF encoding puts the 7-bit code point in an 8-bit field, sometimes called the Network Virtual Terminal or NVT encoding.
sections.eli5: Long ago every country made its own secret code for letters. Unicode is one big shared code book now, and UTF-8 is the way of writing it down that the internet likes best.

sections.title: Character Issues: Normalization, Case and Collation
sections.content:
A code point is a value in the codespace of a repertoire. A combining character attaches to the preceding base character, so "a with acute" can be one precomposed code point or two code points. Normalization unifies such alternatives so two strings can be compared for equivalence, for example n plus combining tilde (U+006E U+0303) versus the single n with tilde (U+00F1). If a protocol wants them treated as equal, it must define where normalization happens. Unicode NFC and NFD support canonical equivalence; NFKC and NFKD support canonical and compatibility equivalence.

Case mapping is not always one-to-one. The RFC cites the Turkish dotless "i", the German sharp S and the Greek final sigma, and says mapping can depend on locale. Converting to a single case for comparison is case folding.

Collation orders strings. It is often specific to a language or locale, and code point order is rarely how a person expects strings to be ordered. Sorting by code point also looks inconsistent if strings are not normalized first.

Unicode is open-ended, with new characters and sometimes new scripts added every year or so. A Unicode subset must therefore be defined by Unicode properties or tied to an identified Unicode version.
sections.eli5: A letter with an accent can be written as one piece or as two pieces stuck together. Normalization picks one way so a computer sees that they are the same.

sections.title: Types of Characters and Subsets
sections.content:
The RFC lists several character types for application designers, while noting they do not neatly divide every character. They include alphabetic and ideographic characters, digits, punctuation, symbols, nonspacing characters, diacritics and control characters. The control characters are the 65 characters in U+0000..U+001F and U+007F..U+009F. Formatting characters are invisible but affect neighbouring characters, such as those that set text direction.

Compatibility characters exist mainly for compatibility with existing character sets. An example is U+FF01 FULLWIDTH EXCLAMATION MARK. The IETF has found it useful to map some groups of compatibility equivalents but not others.

The RFC also clarifies a term in common use: non-ASCII strictly means characters outside the ASCII repertoire, whatever the encoding. The imprecise term "Latin characters" should be avoided, and "Basic Latin" should not be used as a synonym for "ASCII".
sections.eli5: Characters come in kinds: letters, numbers, marks, invisible helper characters and more. Knowing which kind you have tells you how to treat it.

sections.title: Text Entry, Display and Use in Protocols
sections.content:
An input method lets a person enter text. Typical keyboards cannot produce many characters in one stroke, and there are dozens of input methods for Han characters. Rendering rules decide how to display a string. In Arabic the form of a letter depends on its neighbours, Indic scripts may display characters in a different order from how they are stored, and Arabic and Hebrew mix directions. This mixing of left-to-right and right-to-left text is bidirectional display, or bidi. It confuses protocol writers because stored order can differ from screen order, and text with explicit direction characters needs careful processing before sorting or comparison.

In protocols, the names of protocol elements, such as SMTP verbs, are rarely appropriate to internationalize. Protocols that allow more than one charset in the same place should require charset identification, and some, like MIME and HTTP, allow language identification too (see RFC 5646). Transfer encodings such as Base64 and quoted-printable let non-ASCII data pass over legacy channels; the RFC says quoted-printable is jokingly called "quoted unreadable". An ASCII-compatible encoding (ACE) is a way to carry any ISO/IEC 10646 string in the preferred domain name syntax, and only the one produced by Punycode (RFC 3492) has become an IETF standard.
sections.eli5: Some writing goes right to left, and some letters change shape depending on their neighbours. Software has to cope with that, and so do rules for how programs swap text.

sections.title: Internationalized Domain Name Terms
sections.content:
The current specification for internationalized domain names is IDNA2008, whose definitions are in RFC 5890. The RFC lists its specialized terms, including A-label, U-label, LDH label and IDN, without repeating them. An LDH label is the classic DNS label of ASCII letters, digits and hyphens.

Two terms come from the earlier IDNA2003. Stringprep (RFC 3454) is a model and character tables for preparing internationalized strings; it is no longer used in IDNA but is still used in profiles by other protocols. Punycode is the algorithm that converts IDN labels from Unicode to an ACE, though it is often used loosely for the encoded strings.

The word variant began as the relationship between Traditional and Simplified Chinese characters. It now also covers visually confusable characters (ASCII l and 1, or Latin and Cyrillic a), characters with more than one code point, digits of different scripts and orthographic differences like "color" and "colour". The RFC asks that local text say which meaning it intends.
sections.eli5: Web addresses can now use letters from many alphabets. Some letters look alike, so the rules need names for all the different ways two names can look or mean the same.

sections.title: Other Terms and Changes From RFC 3536
sections.content:
The last section is a grab bag. Locale is the user-specific location and cultural information a computer manages, including things like currency, date and time formats. The RFC calls its problems "thorny, unsolved", for example whose locale applies to a piece of text. Romanization is transliteration into Latin characters and is often inexact. Transliteration is usually letter-by-letter and often reversible, while transcription writes down sounds and is almost never round-trip. In ISO/IEC 10646, Han characters were unified, giving fewer code points but also long disagreement over the side effects. Private use code points are defined by the parties using them and are not appropriate for standardization.

Compared with RFC 3536, this document changes status to BCP, adds synonyms, adds the IDNA2008 term list, discusses "variant", adds Unicode subsets (Section 4.2) and the term "writing style", and expands case folding and mapping. It obsoletes RFC 3536.

On security, the document says it is not discussed directly, but comparing tokens that may be text means these concepts matter. It points to the security considerations of RFC 3454, RFC 3629, RFC 4013 and RFC 5890.
sections.eli5: The leftovers are more words about places and language settings, and a list of what was updated since the older version of this dictionary.
